prime.problem: Threads share the heap, so two of them can read the same counter, both add 1 and both write back: one increment vanishes with no error. The bug depends on timing, so it appears only sometimes and hides from tests. Something has to make the read-to-write stretch run one thread at a time.
prime.fits: First card of the Synchronization part. It takes the shared heap from the threads card and shows its price; mutexes, semaphores and monitors (next) are all refinements of the lock introduced here.
expect: why += survived with the GIL, and why that's luck
prime.goal: Reproduce a lost-update race, explain it from an interleaving, fix it with a lock, and say why relying on the GIL is not a fix.

attend: In the two-thread trace, at exactly which step does thread 2's value become stale, and why doesn't it notice?
Why did the sleep(0) version lose 75% of its updates, while plain c["n"] += 1 lost none on 3.10?
What makes a lock's own acquire safe from the same race that a plain busy flag suffers?
Which three ways of avoiding a lock does the card suggest, and what does each give up?
Why is "it passed my tests" weak evidence that code without a lock is correct?

must: Read-modify-write is several steps → a switch between read and write lets another thread write in between → the late writer overwrites with a stale value → lost update (100,096 of 400,000 kept)
A lock makes the read-to-write stretch a critical section → only one thread inside at a time → the interleaving can't split it → all 400,000 kept

The GIL hands off only at certain bytecode points (loop back-edges, function calls) → the eight bytecodes of += ran whole → no losses on 3.10 → but a call or I/O between read and write, or no GIL at all (3.14t: 72.9% lost), brings the race back
A lock must itself be taken atomically → built on a hardware instruction like compare-and-swap → a software flag's check-then-set is two steps and races exactly like the counter
elevated: Uncontended acquire+release is 58 ns → cheap enough to use freely → the real cost is contention, which serialises the critical section (the mutexes card)
reference: the eight bytecode names of c["n"] += 1 on 3.10
the 263,642 of 800,000 run with a 1 µs switch interval

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the four-row no-lock interleaving that turns two increments into c = 1, then redraw it with a lock. In one sentence each, explain why the GIL hid the bug for plain += and why that is not a guarantee.
checklist: both threads read the same old value before either writes
the second write overwrites the first: one update lost
a lock makes read + write one indivisible critical section
the lock itself relies on an atomic instruction
the GIL happens not to switch inside +=, an implementation detail that 3.14t removes

retrieve.q: Explain what a critical section is, using the card's counter, and why a lock around only the write is not enough.
answer: the critical section is the whole read-to-write stretch on shared state
if only the write is locked, two threads can still read the same value before either writes
both then write v + 1, one overwrites the other: the update is still lost

retrieve.q: Walk through why the sleep(0) version kept about a quarter of the updates, step by step for four threads.
answer: each thread reads c, then sleep(0) releases the GIL
the others run and read the same c before anyone writes
all four then write the same c + 1, so four increments count as one
the card flags this as a reading of the ~25% survival, not a measurement

retrieve.q: A teammate says: "CPython has a GIL, so our counters don't need locks." Give the two counter-examples from the card and the cheapest correct alternative.
answer: any call or I/O between the read and the write lets the GIL change hands (the sleep(0) run lost 75%)
free-threaded 3.14t has no GIL: plain += kept 1,082,391 of 4,000,000
a Lock costs 58 ns uncontended; or avoid sharing: per-thread counters summed at the end, or a queue

compare.q: A lock vs a compare-and-swap retry loop for the same counter: what happens to the stale write in each, which design choice causes the difference, and how does each fail under heavy contention?
answer: lock: nobody else reads until the holder writes, so no stale value exists
CAS: the stale write is attempted, detected (the value changed) and redone
lock waiters sleep; CAS losers spin on retries (3,385 retries for 40,000 increments in the demo)
locks fail by contention and deadlock; CAS fails by burning CPU and by ABA on pointers

compare.q: A lost update here and a double charge there both come from two actors acting on stale knowledge. What does each course use to make the second attempt harmless?
answer: here: mutual exclusion, so the second thread reads only after the first has written
there: an idempotency key, so a repeated request is recognised and not applied twice
a lock needs shared memory and a cheap atomic; across machines you can't lock cheaply, so you make repeats safe instead

predict.q: In asyncio, one coroutine does v = c["n"], then await asyncio.sleep(0), then c["n"] = v + 1, and 4 tasks run it 10⁵ times each. There is only one thread and no GIL hand-off between tasks. Do updates get lost? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Yes, and for the same reason as the sleep(0) thread version: the await is a switch point between the read and the write, so another task reads the same value first. The card says so directly: a read, then an await, then a write still races. Remove the await between them and no task can interleave, so nothing is lost without a lock.

apply.task: Break and fix code/locks.py three ways and record the final count each time (4 threads × 10⁵): (1) put the lock around the write only; (2) remove sleep(0) from the unlocked version but call a tiny Python function def g(v): return v between the read and the write; (3) drop sharing entirely: give each thread its own counter and sum at the end.
apply.done: Run 1 and run 2 lose updates (count below 400,000), run 3 gives exactly 400,000 with no lock, and you can say for each which step of the interleaving explains it.
apply.hint: The card's own run with a Python call between read and write kept 263,642 of 800,000 at a 1 µs switch interval; at the default 5 ms your losses may be much smaller, so run it a few times or lower sys.setswitchinterval.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the asyncio race, or which of your three breaks lost updates?
Can you explain the lost update from the interleaving, without saying "threads are unsafe"?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: GIL hand-off points → why += survived, or atomic instruction → why a lock is safe?
How would you now test code for a race it only shows sometimes?
What will you look for in the mutexes card: what a lock costs when it's contended rather than free?
